size.note: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), gives mean forearm length as 2.91 ± 0.11 cm in females and 2.87 ± 0.11 cm in males, and maximum forearm length as 3.12 cm in females and 2.99 cm in males. It notes slight sexual dimorphism, with females slightly heavier than males, but publishes no mass figures. Wikipedia, citing Branch and Stuart (2007), gives an average mass of 3.5 g (0.0035 kg) and remarks that the species is perhaps Africa's smallest bat. No head-and-body length, total length, tail length, wingspan or mass range was published on the pages used.

summary: A very small insect-eating vesper bat of savanna woodland, usually near water, with bicoloured fur that has rusty-tinged tips and pale rusty-grey bases. It is a clutter-edge forager that takes beetles, flies and moths. Daytime roosts are poorly known, but it has been found in tree crevices and hollows, under the bark of dead Vachellia trees, and in the roof spaces of old buildings. The 2025 regional assessment rates it Least Concern. That page does not mention Kruger National Park; it lists occurrence in the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park and gives the movement pattern as unknown.
description: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), says the species can sometimes be distinguished from other similarly sized pipistrelles in the field by its bicoloured fur, which has rusty-tinged tips and pale rusty-grey bases, and that males are readily identifiable from other pipistrelle-like bats by their distinctive penile morphology (Fasel et al. 2020). The English checklist name is Rusty bat, and the Afrikaans checklist name is Roeskleurvlermuis; those list forms are kept here. The 2025 EWT assessment uses Rusty Bat as its title and also lists Rusty Pipistrelle, Rusty Pipistrelle Bat and Rustic Pipistrelle, with the Afrikaans name Roeskleurvlermuis. Wikipedia's title, and iNaturalist's preferred English name, is Rusty pipistrelle. The species was described as Scotophilus rusticus Tomes, 1861; the current combination is Pipistrellus rusticus. The assessment also lists Pipistrellus marrensis Thomas and Hinton, 1923 and Eptesicops rusticus Roberts, 1926 as synonyms. It notes that two subspecies have been recognised (Simmons 2005), P. r. marrensis from Senegal to Ethiopia and Kenya and the slightly larger P. r. rusticus in southern Africa, but that the validity of these subspecies is uncertain, and that recent molecular work (Torrent et al. 2025) suggests southern African individuals are more closely related to Pipistrellus cf. hesperidus from Senegal than to Kenyan P. hesperidus. Those taxonomic points are flagged, not used to remap the checklist name. The 2025 assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), gives mean forearm length as 2.91 cm in females and 2.87 cm in males. Wikipedia, citing Branch and Stuart (2007), gives an average mass of 3.5 g and remarks that the species is perhaps Africa's smallest bat.
habits: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), says there are limited data on roosting habits, but that the species is commonly netted over water and has been collected in tree crevices and hollows (Roberts 1951; Taylor 2000), under the bark of dead Vachellia (previously Acacia) trees (Rautenbach 1982), and in roof spaces in old buildings (Skinner and Chimimba 2005). It is a clutter-edge forager. Individuals in the assessment region may roost in small colonies; such behaviour has been documented in tree-roosting colonies in Zambia (Taylor 2000). Movement patterns are listed as Unknown. It has low wing loading (Norberg and Rayner 1987).

diet.summary: An insectivore. The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Aldridge and Rautenbach (1987), says it is a clutter-edge forager with a diet of beetles (Coleoptera), flies (Diptera) and moths (Lepidoptera). As an insectivore it may help control crop pests in macadamia agroecosystems (Weier et al. 2021; Boyles et al. 2011; Kunz et al. 2011).

young: The 2025 EWT assessment states that the species gives birth to live young. It exhibits seasonal monoestry: copulation occurs in April, females store sperm until ovulation and fertilisation in August and September, and births occur in November (van der Merwe and Rautenbach 1990; van der Merwe and Mostert 2005). Gestation time is given as approximately 3–4 months (van der Merwe and Mostert 2005). Females give birth to two pups each season (van der Merwe and Mostert 2005). Those reproductive remarks come from studies in Limpopo and the northern Transvaal bushveld. Generation length, age at maturity, size at birth and longevity are listed as unknown or not specified. Pup appearance was not described on the pages used.

predators.note: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Malan et al. (2022), documents predation by bat hawks (Macheiramphus alcinus). Not a mammal in this guide.

prey.note: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Aldridge and Rautenbach (1987), reports a diet of Coleoptera, Diptera and Lepidoptera. Not mammals in this guide.

habitat: The 2025 EWT assessment, citing Monadjem et al. (2020), says the species inhabits savanna woodland and has a strong association with water sources, but is absent from both mesic miombo woodlands and xeric savanna. It has been captured along the riparian fringes of the Wilge River in a heterogeneous grassland-dominated landscape (de Jong et al. 2025). Within the assessment region it occurs in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, Gauteng, the North West and Eswatini (Monadjem et al. 2020). Ecological niche models suggest a broader potential distribution across the eastern parts of the assessment region, mainly in grassland and savannah biomes, largely excluding low-lying coastal habitats (Monadjem et al. 2010). Elevation limits are given as 6–2,527 m above sea level (Monadjem et al. 2024). The conservation section says it is protected in more than ten conservation areas in the assessment region, including the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park, the Greater Mapungubwe Transfrontier Conservation Area and Madikwe Nature Reserve. The page does not name Kruger National Park.

population.notes: No Kruger census or SANParks park-wide count was found. The 2025 regional assessment lists the current population trend as Stable, does not give a Kruger figure, and says that although the distribution is patchy the species is considered locally common (Van der Merwe and Rautenbach 1990; ACR 2024), for example in mopane woodland with rocky Clarens sandstones in the Limpopo valley (Monadjem et al. 2020). It is well represented in museums, with more than 150 specimens examined in Monadjem et al. (2020). The assessment also states that the effective population size is likely to exceed 500 if the species is part of a large metapopulation in the assessment region and adjacent countries. Those remarks apply to South Africa, Eswatini and Lesotho, not to Kruger.

viewNotes.note: A clutter-edge forager, commonly netted over water. The 2025 EWT assessment notes low wing loading (Norberg and Rayner 1987).

Roosting habits are poorly known. It has been collected in tree crevices and hollows, under the bark of dead Vachellia trees, and in roof spaces of old buildings, and may roost in small tree-roosting colonies.

research.note: This file follows species-list.json in treating the Kruger-list animal as Pipistrellus rusticus (English Rusty bat; Afrikaans Roeskleurvlermuis) and does not remap the name. Wikipedia and iNaturalist use Rusty pipistrelle as the preferred English name; the 2025 EWT assessment uses Rusty Bat as its title and also lists Rusty Pipistrelle. Those alternatives are flagged here, not used to change the checklist name. The 2025 assessment, citing Torrent et al. (2025) and Simmons (2005), notes that southern African individuals may be more closely related to Pipistrellus cf. hesperidus from Senegal than to Kenyan P. hesperidus, and that the validity of the subspecies P. r. marrensis and P. r. rusticus is uncertain; those points are flagged, not used to split or remap the checklist taxon. The 2025 page names the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park but does not mention Kruger National Park, and its range remarks (occurrence in Limpopo, Mpumalanga, Gauteng, the North West and Eswatini) are not stated in Lowveld terms. Movement patterns are listed as Unknown, which does not by itself block resident status. A research-grade iNaturalist search in Kruger (place 69020) returned no observations. Status and monthsPresent are omitted even though the species is on the 2011 Kruger checklist.

gaps: The 2025 EWT assessment does not mention Kruger National Park (it names the Great Limpopo Transfrontier Park), and it describes occurrence in Limpopo and Mpumalanga but not specifically the Lowveld. Movement patterns are listed as Unknown. A research-grade iNaturalist search in Kruger (place 69020) returned no observations. Status and monthsPresent are omitted because no definite Kruger record was found.
No Kruger census or park-wide count; the 2025 regional assessment lists the regional trend as Stable and discusses regional abundance, not a Kruger figure.
No published head-and-body length, total length, tail length, wingspan or mass range; only mean and maximum forearm lengths, plus a Wikipedia average mass of 3.5 g, were given.
No sourced echolocation or social-call description. No iNaturalist sound was found in Kruger (place 69020).

No licensable photograph was found in Kruger (place 69020), in South Africa (place 6986), or in southern Africa (place 113055). Wikimedia Commons has only File:Pipistrellus rusticus.jpg, a white-background portrait from Mamba et al. (2024), which was not used; a search under the English name Rusty pipistrelle found no further photographs.
Pup appearance was not published in the sources used.
Ear, face, underparts, wing, leg and tail colours were not described on the pages used, beyond bicoloured fur with rusty-tinged tips and pale rusty-grey bases.
No named similar species; the 2025 assessment only notes that the species can be difficult to distinguish in the field from other similarly sized pipistrelles.
